source: original; documents are public-domain primary sources or paraphrases of them (see each document's sourcing note)

books.section: B. The Resistance Movement from Above and from Below

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which colonial resistance to British policies was a unified movement, 1763–1774.

documents.title: The Virginia Resolves
documents.source: Virginia Resolves, House of Burgesses, May 1765. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The assembly adopted the moderate resolves but pulled back from the boldest ones — resistance from above had limits even at the start.
documents.text: Resolved, that the General Assembly of this Colony have the only and sole exclusive right and power to lay Taxes and Impositions upon the inhabitants of this Colony.

documents.title: A crowd attacks Hutchinson's house
documents.source: Account of the attack on Lieutenant Governor Thomas Hutchinson's house, Boston, August 26, 1765. Paraphrased from the course books' accounts.
documents.sourcing: Crowd action, not assembly action — resistance from below, aimed at a man who had defended the Stamp Act.
documents.text: On the night of August 26, 1765, a Boston crowd broke into Lieutenant Governor Thomas Hutchinson's house, smashed his furniture, tore up his papers, and stole his silver. Hutchinson, who had defended the Stamp Act, fled with his family.

documents.title: The Daughters of Liberty spin
documents.source: Account of the Daughters of Liberty and the Edenton Tea Party, 1765-1774. Paraphrased from the course books' accounts.
documents.sourcing: Resistance reaching beyond the assemblies into households — women who could not vote still acted, by making cloth and refusing tea.
documents.text: Women calling themselves the Daughters of Liberty gathered at spinning bees, making cloth at home so their families would not have to buy British goods. In Edenton, North Carolina, 51 women signed a resolve in October 1774 pledging to give up tea and British cloth.

documents.title: John Adams defends the soldiers
documents.source: John Adams, closing argument for the defense in the Boston Massacre trial, December 1770. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Adams was a Patriot leader, yet he defended the accused soldiers — the movement's leaders also insisted on the rule of law.
documents.text: Facts are stubborn things; and whatever may be our wishes, our inclinations, or the dictates of our passion, they cannot alter the state of facts and evidence.

documents.title: The Gaspee is burned
documents.source: Account of the burning of HMS Gaspee, Rhode Island, June 1772. Paraphrased from the course books' accounts.
documents.sourcing: Rhode Islanders acting on their own, with no assembly and no congress behind them — and London unable to punish anyone for it.
documents.text: When the British revenue schooner Gaspee ran aground off Rhode Island in June 1772, colonists rowed out at night, seized the crew, and burned the ship to the waterline. A royal commission investigated, but no one was ever charged.

documents.title: The Boston Tea Party
documents.source: Account of the Boston Tea Party, December 16, 1773. Paraphrased from the course books' accounts.
documents.sourcing: A Boston crowd action, carried out in disguise and in secret, that Parliament answered by punishing the whole colony.
documents.text: On the night of December 16, 1773, men dressed as Mohawk Indians boarded three ships in Boston Harbor and threw about 350 chests of tea into the water. The next morning the tea was gone, and no one in Boston would name the men who had done it.

documents.title: The First Continental Congress
documents.source: Account of the First Continental Congress, Philadelphia, September-October 1774. Paraphrased from the course books' accounts.
documents.sourcing: The first body to speak for nearly all the colonies at once — twelve colonies, with Georgia alone absent — and the closest the resistance came to acting as one.
documents.text: The First Continental Congress met in Philadelphia in September 1774, with delegates from twelve colonies. It adopted the Continental Association — a pledge of nonimportation, nonexportation, and nonconsumption — and set up committees in every town to enforce it.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which colonial resistance to British policies was a unified movement, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of change does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the separate colonies before 1763, each with its own assembly and its own quarrels with London, and no body that spoke for them all.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant evidence from at least three documents to support an argument about change or continuity.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than three documents, or quoting documents without describing what they show, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument, with the evidence accurately described and tied to the claim.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the loyalists who opposed the resistance, the Stamp Act Congress of 1765, or Joseph Galloway's plan of union at the First Continental Congress.
rubric.notEarned: A general statement with no specific example beyond the documents does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document's author, purpose, audience, or historical situation to the argument, for at least two documents, such as the Virginia Resolves as adopted versus the bolder resolves the assembly withdrew, or Adams defending the soldiers he opposed politically.
rubric.notEarned: Identifying an author without explaining why it matters, or sourcing only one document, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the extent of unity, showing that the movement shared a principle but differed in methods and aims, or weighing unity against the divisions inside it.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: Colonial resistance was broadly shared but never uniform: assemblies, crowds, women, and merchants all opposed British taxation on the same principle, yet they acted by different means and for different ends, and only the Coercive Acts of 1774 brought them together in a single body.
Context: Before 1763 the colonies had no body that spoke for them all; each assembly dealt with London on its own, and the colonies often quarreled with one another as much as with Britain.
Evidence: Documents 1 and 7 show resistance from above — the Virginia assembly asserting its sole right to tax, and twelve colonies meeting in Congress to enforce the Association. Documents 2, 3, 5, and 6 show resistance from below — a Boston crowd wrecking Hutchinson's house, women spinning homespun and refusing tea, Rhode Islanders burning the Gaspee, and Bostonians dumping the tea in disguise. Document 4 shows the limits — Adams, a Patriot leader, defending the soldiers his own side called murderers.
Beyond the documents: Not all colonists resisted — loyalists defended Parliament's authority, and at the First Continental Congress Joseph Galloway proposed a plan of union with Britain that the delegates rejected by a single vote.
Sourcing: The Virginia Resolves as adopted are the moderate ones — the assembly withdrew its boldest claims, so the document shows both defiance and caution; Adams's courtroom words carry weight precisely because he was defending men his own movement condemned; the crowd accounts come from the books' summaries, not from the crowds themselves.
Complexity: Unity was real but uneven — the principle of no taxation without representation was shared across the colonies, while the methods ranged from petitions to arson, and the movement unified in 1774 only because Parliament's punishment of Boston made every colony feel the threat; the same resistance that united the colonies also exposed how different they were.
